overview: The atlas label “Minor Hindu Kingdoms” is not the name of a state. Its 1279 outline combines parts of India with Borneo and Sulawesi; its 1300 outline covers India alone. This card uses named Indian examples, especially Hoysala and Kakatiya communities. Their importance was not “minor,” and the label cannot establish everyone’s religion. The island fragments belong to a different regional history.

periods.title: Established regional powers
periods.summary: Hoysala and Kakatiya territories contained older temples, endowed settlements and active regional courts.

periods.title: Political upheaval
periods.summary: Warangal fell to a Delhi army in 1323; Hoysala authority survived into the 1340s.

periods.title: Changing patrons
periods.summary: The map’s final decades should not be read as the survival of one kingdom. Religious institutions later received new patrons.

items.text: At Somanathapura in Karnataka, an inscription dates the village and Keshava temple to 1268, eleven years before this map interval. Somanatha, a senior military officer serving Narasimha III, founded the settlement. Major building projects connected rulers, officers and the agricultural economy.

The Malkapuram record, catalogued as 1261, connects a grant promised by Ganapatideva with the formal gift made by his daughter Rudramadevi. A religious teacher organized its endowments. This earlier Kakatiya example comes from near Guntur, outside the imported outline: women could be central actors in royal patronage.

In 1323, a Delhi Sultanate army captured Warangal and took the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra prisoner. This was a particular dynasty’s defeat. It did not end every regional community or create a single replacement state across the entire map label.

sections.title: Builders, water and stories in stone

items.text: At Palampet, Ramappa temple construction began in 1213, before this map interval. Builders used porous, lightweight bricks in the tower above heavier stonework. The nickname “floating bricks” describes a clever choice of material to reduce roof weight. The tower was not trying to sail away.

Ramappa’s setting includes a Kakatiya reservoir, irrigation works and cultivated fields. Water storage linked farming with the temple landscape. Cultivation and ceremonies shared a carefully arranged landscape: reservoir, channels, fields and buildings belonged in the same picture.

At Halebidu, older temple carvings remained part of the region’s cultural landscape. One scene shows Krishna sheltering a community beneath a mountain: cattle, herders and musicians huddle below, while monkeys and birds occupy the heights. It is a sacred story with remarkably busy details, not a literal weather report.

Somanathapura’s foundation record earmarked revenue for decoration, dancing and daily or seasonal festivals. Behind a celebration stood an endowment and people doing paid or supported work. A beautifully carved temple also required an ongoing operating budget.

Halebidu inscriptions from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries record donations by both men and women from different occupations and social backgrounds. Offerings included flowers, food, scented water and lamp light. Religious life involved many contributors beyond the royal family.

As a nearby comparison outside the atlas outline, Malkapuram’s endowed community included more than sixty Brahmin families, teachers, cooks, artisans and a physician. Supporting learning and ritual required numerous practical jobs. This is a record of one organized settlement, not a census of all medieval families.

The same Malkapuram endowment included a feeding house whose provision was described as serving people regardless of caste or creed. Land revenue was assigned to maintain it. Shared meals were a concrete charitable purpose, even in a society with pronounced social divisions.

sections.title: Learning, health and an authentic written word

items.text: An inscription dated 1300 describes Somanathapura as a settlement of learned Brahmins. Earlier foundations and later grants show how a place could combine worship with scholarly residence. This documents a particular learned community, not schooling for every child.

In the nearby Malkapuram comparison, the thirteenth-century inscription names medical institutions. Scholar Dominik Wujastyk transcribes ārogyaśālā, meaning “hospital,” and prasūtiśāla, “birthing house.” These are Sanskrit words in modern scholarly Roman transcription. The source establishes named facilities, rather than their treatment success or a surviving modern-style ward.

At that Malkapuram foundation, land was divided to support the temple, students and monastery, and charitable institutions including maternity and general medical care. The record allotted shares to a physician and an administrative worker. Care depended on a financial arrangement, not only on a generous promise.

A separate comparison at Palakol, outside this outline, comes from 1300. An inscription names Vasudeva as skilled in treating horses and identifies his father Anantapandita as a horse physician too. It gives a small glimpse of medical expertise within a family, although it does not describe their lessons or remedies.

Malkapuram’s evidence is physically substantial: its pillar carries about 200 lines across three sides. Sanskrit verse forms most of the text, while Telugu supplies details such as village boundaries. A monument can preserve practical administration alongside praise of its patrons.

An earlier coastal comparison is Motupalli’s edict of 1244 to 1245, outside this atlas outline. It promised foreign merchants that shipwrecked cargo would face ordinary customs duties rather than wholesale seizure. A royal inscription could address the alarming practical question: what happens to your goods when your ship wrecks?

ending.text: There was no collective collapse in 1400. Kakatiya rule ended in 1323, while Hoysala power ended in the 1340s. At Somanathapura, later Vijayanagara and Nayaka patrons supported repairs and grants. Communities and institutions continued under changing authorities; the atlas endpoint is a mapping limit.
